newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Armed troops deploy to guard Algerian voters.
newsitem.headline: Armed troops deploy to guard Algerian voters.

text.p: Heavily armed troops and police started to deploy around polling stations in Algiers on Wednesday as millions of voters throughout Algeria prepared for their first general election in over five years of violence and bloodshed.

The security deployment for Thursday's ballot followed a wave of bombings blamed on Moslem fundamentalists -- the latest on Monday -- in which at least 22 people were killed and 120 wounded in three days.

Markets and many schools are shut, draconian no-parking measures are being enforced and appeals for the public to be alert for suspicious packages or vehicles are further parts of the security effort being made by the authorities.
The authorities are expected to deploy around 200,000 soldiers and other security forces to guard the nearly 16.8 million voters among Algeria's 29 million people.
The ballot is seen by President Liamine Zeroual as a key to ending years of crisis that followed the last general election in December 1991.
Then, the now-outlawed Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) dominated the poll and in January 1992 the authorities scrapped it. Algeria plunged into violence in which about 60,000 people have died.
Two staunch anti-Islamist newspapers on Wednesday warned voters against giving the two legal Islamist-oriented parties a substantial representation in the new parliament.
Under the headline "The spectre of December 1991", Le Matin said moderate Islamists of the Movement of a Peaceful Society (MPS) and Nahda parties were already "singing the victory song".
"If Islamists win tomorrow, it will be back to 1991."
El Assil daily said the MPS, led by Mahfoud Nahnah, was trying to "infiltrate democracy" and steal a win for Islamists.
More than 7,700 candidates representing 39 political parties are vying for the 380-seat National Assembly (lower house).
The authorities have called for a high turnout in this vast, oil and gas producing country. The FIS has called for a boycott.
Analysts expect the MPS to do well but they tip the National Democratic Rally (RND), which gathers pro-government supporters, to emerge as the leading party in parliament.
Other key parties include the Socialist Forces Front of secularist opposition leader Hocine Ait Ahmed and the Rally for Culture and Democracy of anti-Islamist Said Saadi.
A new proprotional representation law virtually guarantees that at least four or five parties will be in parliament with little chance of a single party holding an absolute majority.

Zeroual, quoted by the official Algerian media, said late on Tuesday he expected a high turnout despite Moslem rebel attacks which he said were aimed at spreading fear and doubt in the hearts of Algerians.
"I am convinced...that despite these terrorist acts the Algerian people will vote in large numbers," he said in Harare, Zimbabwe, where he was attending an African summit.
Western diplomats and local analysts say the election should be free and fair to stand any chance of starting a process to resolve the crisis.

"We have no hope that the election itself will end the violence but we hope that a credible election will be a first step towards political reforms opening the door for more reforms," said one diplomat.
